FUTURE SPACE EVENTS: EXPLANATORY NOTES

The various lists and calendars of events are presented in a preliminary
way and are meant to illustrate the nature of certain final productions. They
were, in fact, literally written in a hurry and without consultation of facts
which will later be turned to for the sake of criticism and refinement. This
is not to suggest, however, that the dates and events are not censidered or
are overly foolish. The blatant and indefensible errors are presumably rare.

The question naturally arises whether the events and dates have much
chance of being accurate, no matter how well done. Is the author gifted with
prophetic powers such that his schedule of events represents absolute
foreknowledge about the unique and unalterable course of things? The answer is
that there are an infinity of worthwhile schedules, all different, that could
be made. That is, the very attempt to confer some reasonable order and pattern
upon all possible events is beneficial and enlightening. The hypothetical
calendar created in this daring way is a temptation to all kinds of criticism,
as well as being a challenge to man's larger program. It prompts revisions
and alternatives. It feels events out in an intuitive way. It casts at least
one man's perspective in a chronological mold. Even if the exact chronology
is defective, something of the larger order and pattern may not be. Events
in the future of space are clearly extraordinarily contingent upon political,
military, social, technical, and purely spacial developments. Yet there is an
opportunity for devising a sequence fairly independent of such contingencies
whose pace and sequencing is educational and persuasive, and can to some extent
be relied on in the face of such (frustrative or acceleratory) contingencies.

The events and dates are useful in another important respect. They
supply a story to, and dramatize, what may in fact or in effect occur. On
a scale of possibilities within 200 years an evolutionary imagery has the effect
of justifying nearer events by relating them to a larger, more impressive, and
more meaningful framework. Space exploration and development is shown to have
a start and a proper continuation. Maintenance and growth of man's spacial
enterprise is rendered sensible. Initial exploration and development are
identified with important consequences. Sadly, this has never been done. It
has been made to seem that things done in space and yet to be done are smal}
and arbitrary. The result has been minor interest in space programs and
unreliable support. The space program in general has yet to fulfill itself
and the nature of fulfillment has never been depicted.

"A General Calendar for the Future of Space'': comments on. Each "event"!
designated in this calendar might as well be prefaced by the words: ''If the
event is going to occur, it might reasonably occur by...'' Such a thought
doubtless preoccupied me as | dated and arranged the events. There was
obviously, also, a competition between date-of-feasibility and date-of-actual-
occurrence, a conflict which mars the overall chronology. As long as the
user remains sensible of such factors, however, their effect is not apt to
be catastrophic, and the calendar will serve its imperfect role.

It is noteworthy that on the longer scale of time the calendar may be
more realistic since the extrinsic and unpredictable factors influencing
spacial events in the nearer term, say within 50 years or by 2025, may lose
something of their turbulence and subside after 2025 and/or smoothed over bigger
units of time.

The events are listed in the following way. They run from the past to
the eschatological year 100,000,000,000 A.D. This seemed a sufficient scope.
First, a reasonable year at or by which the event should transpire is given
(sometimes more than one year is given). Occasionally the year is preceded
by a question mark. This signifies that there is a serious question whether

the event will occur at all (perhaps it is infeasible, pointless, or conjectural).
Occasionally the year is followed by a question mark. This means that the date,
per se, is somehow suspicious. The event may actually deserve an earlier or a
later date, or a date refined into subpossibilities and alternatives.

Secondly, the event itself is identified. The identification given is
actually an abstraction from another document, "Annotated Calendar for the Future
of Space'’. This last is being continuously revised and extended. It should be
resorted to wherever difficulties and questions arise in examining the
breviloquent calendar presently under discussion. This is readily done since,
thirdly, the statement of each ewent Is succeeded by a cross-referential number.

Finally, each such number is followed by a range. The interval of time
thereby indicated is that | at first assigned the events (but with which |
sometimes later disagreed). ! have included these intervals because they
supplement, and in some cases are more interesting than, the specific dates |
have, having been asked to do so, assigned to the events (even the intervals,
of course, are questionable). 1! have here and there appended sharps, #, to
the intervals. These signify that a range of possibilities or a set of subevents
belong to, and properly divide, the event as given. Similarly, at the beginning

date of the line | have occasionally added the initials 'gc''. In this case what
is meant is that a continuum of possible or actual dates probably obtains, and
that the user should not be deceived. I have, finally, put some dates in

quotes~-eg ''1988''--by way of admitting that the nature of the event, as or even
as worded, was not clear to me, so that the date chosen was somewhat arbitrary
or expedient.

Matters that are obscure, controversial, important, &rc--in both the abbreviated
and annotatory calendars--!I intend to elaborate on in a future series of notes
incorperated in the annotated calendar or occurring as brief, independent papers.

Is the pace of events set forth in my calendars too slow or too hasty? |
concede at once that it may happen that mankind, over the next few decades, will
basically turn its back on outer space and concern itself with more down-to-Earth
problems and opportunities. Whereas | do not think this will happen, | do think
there will be 1-2 or 1-3 decades of restraint over the world, and some ignoration
of larger possibilities. Also, there are a set of likely or unlikely things which
might restore or enlarge an interest in space, say over the next 3 decades, and
impose themselves on the natural background of temporary neglect.

The pace of events | have assumed presupposes exponential progress in human
affairs, generally, and to some extent also in space. As such it is merely
consistent with continued exponential growth or a reasonable logistic curve
moderating future growth. Even if world demographic and economic growth begins
to turn over and obey a logistic curve in the future, there is good reason to
think that scientific progress will lag or disobey such an inflection and will
continue to accelerate or maintain approximately its current rate, and certainly
there are some affairs (of which the space program may prove an example) which
should behave in this optimistic way.

If the exploration and development of outer space continues in a serious and
vigorous way, the rate of change and evolution | have given to events is perfectly
reasonable. Modern progress in science, technology, engineering, and other human
accomplishment is really extraordinarily fast. Both prospectively and retrospectively
it is almost incomprehensible. Were space pursued with enthusiasm or abandon
my calendar would probably prove to have been very conservative. The timing of
the entire calendar, therefore, is critically dependent upon a good estimate of
future human motivation and whatever things this, in turn, is dependent on.

The scale of the calendars. The warrant for a bicentennial prospect, beyond
my previous remarks, is that 2 centuries (between now and 2176) actually seems
to correspond to the period of the initial beginning of the solar system as a
multiplanetary civilization. Almost all of the potential evehts | have identified

GLOSSARY
AEROSPACE Operating in both air and Space.
BAMBI Ballistic Missile Boost Intercept. Orbital] missile-interception systems
that would be used to attack: launched missiles at their vulnerable "boost!
phase.

INTRASPAC IAL Of that within space and off bodies.

SPACIAL Of outer space.

O'NEILL COLONY, TERRAN L-5, &C At two points 60° ahead of and 60° behind Moon
in its orbit about Earth dynamical stability exists with respect to the gravity
of these two bodies. These two Lagrangian points, L-4 and L-5, invite
colonization by man, as has been Proposed and developed by physicist Gerard
K. O'Neill. O'Neill visualizes them as populable by millions of men, as
sites for large-scale industries, and as way stations for other points in
Solar System. He specifically visualizes their emergence between 1982 and
2020. It is not inconceivable that considerable matter exists naturally at
these loci. This pair of points also exists for the Sun-Earth system, for
the Sun-Jupiter system (the Trojan Planets), &c.

ARTIFICIAL MOON A huge reflector distributed or erected in space in order to
redirect sunlight to Earth, eg to diminish nocturnal darkness, raise
temperatures at high latitudes, &c.

RERELUNAR Located on the backside of Moon.

SUPER ATMOSPHERES Atmospheres with supernorma] oxygen, pressure, or the like.
Hypothetically, these might improve agriculture when this is done off Earth
in the future.

EXOBIOLOGICAL ACCIDENT Some disaster resulting from or involving extraterrestrial
organisms. An example would be a Terran pandemic produced by a pathogen
returned from a planet visited by man, cf The Andromeda Strain, a novel by
Michael Crichton. Conversely, a Terran Organism might ravage what biology
was previously found on the other planet.

HOLLOWED ASTEROID Dandridge M. Cole and Donald W. Cox, in their book Islands
In Space, The Challenge of the Planetoids, suggested that elliptical asteroids of
moderate size might be hollowed out, Spun, and inhabited. The spin would
give them artificial gravity, the mural landscape could be planted, farmed,
and built upon, an artificial atmosphere could be created, along with an
artificial sun down -the major axis; Such a nice intraspacial microcosm is
vividly depicted in Rendezvous With Rama, a novel by Arthur C. Clarke.

DYSONIAN Engineering or construction on a nearly, actually, or more than planetary
scale in terms of mass, energy, population, time, &r the like is called
"Dysonian" after the eminent physicist Freeman Dyson.

DYSON SPHERE The eminent physicist Freeman Dysoh-has seriously proposed that
man in the future may build i; rotating band around Sun in order to capture
and make use of the total 104! erg/y emission that is otherwise being
constantly lost to Universe. Jupiter, which has 340 X the mass of Earth,
could provide: the necessary material. Dyson suggests that such surfaces
may already exist about other Stars, the creations of other civilizations.

ARTIFICIAL PLANETS Buildings of planetary size (eg 1076-192 ) built at once
or incrementally in space out of available materials. Natural planets are
too dense and hot inside to be developed at great depth. So the Proper
thing to do is to take them apart and build low density, highly vacuous,
and completely artificial Structures, either flat or spherical. In this
way the inhabitable surface can be multiplied tremendously, eg 100,000 x.

CELESTIAL PHOTONICS There may be created in space in the future actual or
virtual lenses, mirrors, basers, transformers, transducers, modulators,
capacitors, batteries, conductors, resistors, and other circuitry of titanic
Or astronomic scale for proportionate applications of the annual 10 erg

solar efflux of photons. These innumerable photons could be used for
planetary engineering, communication, scientific instruments of observation,
and many other purposes of a kind and scale utterly beyond our puny grasp.

CUTOSPHERE .and’ TENT. It is not unlikely that other planetaries will come to
be covered with great numbers of inflated and thin-shell domes sheltering
men and their cities in local atmospheres. It may happen that these will
eventually grow so numerous as to touch one another and emerge as domes
of ever greater magnitude. It may also happen that men will desire to
create or alter entire atmospheres of planets in single bold steps. The
result in either case may be the enclosure of the whole planetary ina
low-and-closed skin, or "cutosphere'’", Perhaps 10-100 ft high, such bagged
atmospheres might be far more efficient, economical, Stable, regulable,
natural, practical, &¢ than ordinary gradient atmospheres. The magnitudinous
sequence, again, would be: dome, tent, cutosphere.

VON NEUMANN MACHINES. The journalist Adrian Berry, in his book The Next Ten
Thousand Years, A Vision of Man's Future in the Universe, discusses what
is actually the technological vision of the physicist Freeman Dyson, in
turn referring to the seminal ideas of the mathematical genius John von
Neumann. Von Neumann was concerned, before he died in 1957, with abstract
and physical entities possessing life's essential properties of
self-reproduction, multiplication, maintenance, growth, and evolution.

Such entities have come to be called ''cellular automata''. The development
and application of this field will surely be one of the most thrilling
chapters in the history of the intellect. Dyson realized that cellular
automata possess cosmoplastic (ie world changing) and cosmopoietic (ie
world creating) properties. They literally offer an infinite potential

to remake Universe. Suppose an automaton were produced that could fend

for itself anywhere in Universe, reproduce itself and do so as quickly as
possible, evolve to meet any conditions, and that somehow possessed the
ultimate ambitions of filling, conquering, and transforming Universe.
Suppose one were freed on Moon. Spreading and evolving exponentially,

it would, with remarkable speed, achieve just those incredible ambitions!
(Indeed, it is thought that what we call the natural universe may be merely
the pageantry of such automata, as has been suggested by computer scientist
Edward Fredkin.) Dyson has therefore suggested that man will one day have
created cellular automata, or artificial biota, engineered for particular,
grand purposes, such as the speedy refashioning of an entire planet, a
level of automation utterly beyond any semblance of that ours today. By
way of example, in centuries, or even mere decades, the whole atmosphere
of Venus could be terraformed.

TERRAFORMING, -PLANETURGY,“and ECOPOIESIS Terraforming refers to the adaptation
of large-scale, especially planetary, environment to human needs by remodel ing
it along Terran lines. Planeturgy refers to any changing or creation of
environments of the order of size of the face of a planetary, whether
climatic, atmospheric, hydrologic, geologic, biologic, érc. Finally, eco-
polesis to the creation of some environment. Another customary term is
PLANETARY ENGINEERING, a synonym for planeturgy. Although what is usually
intended by these terms is some alteration of a planetary surface, they
comprehend as well any great deeds performed upon planetary interiors.

PERITERRESTRIAL Of that region of space beyond the atmosphere, and yet in the
vicinnity, of Earth. It especially refers to Earth-orbital and geocentric
activities. (The prefix "peri-'' is used similarly for other systems.)

EXTRATERRESTRIAL Of, relating to, or characterizing that space beyond Earth's
atmosphere, or even beyond periterrestrial space.

TRANSLUMINARY Pertaining to that which is faster than light (>c).

PLENISTIC PHYSICS A realm of physics that may evolve in the future if nature

is variously found to be of unsuspectedly great, or of infinite,
subdivision, structure, density, energy, dimensionality, complexity,
hierarchy, variability, &rc. Possibilities here are themselves infinite,
but some of those now living who have had ideas of this kind are P.A.M.
Dirac, John A. Wheeler, Fred Hoyle, H.C. Dudley, Gerald Feinberg, and
Patrick Gunkel. For example, it may be that all but 1% of the mass of
Universe is invisible (neutrinos or black holes), that "real!! energy and
mass are infinitesimal alongside the energy density of the so-called
vacuum, that the material and energic density of any space-time point

is infinite or superinfinite owing i.a. to the bidirectionally infinite
frequency and energy spectra of nature, &rc. Such physics may lead

to progressive scientific discovery and applications in terms of usable
-resources, transportation, communication, exploration, inventions, &rc.

TELEPORTATION Any technological analogue to the parapsychological concept
of material things being moved through space immaterially. Specifically,
telefacsimilization of objects reproducing to some degree their appearance,
constitution, or even chemistry--eg via 10°72 bits/gram--and invading
thereby the realm of so-called communication. The velocity of transmission
might range from greater than, at, or less than the speed of light. The
rapidity of terminal conversion might range from less than a second to
months. The presumable idea is that, with or without simplification,
the character of the object is transformed into, or transmitted as, pure
information &r energy, and is thus received and rematerialized. But
there exists the possibility that something like ''superspace'’ might enable
an object qua object to be shifted discontinuously and instantaneously
through space-time, sans strict conversion or any simplification.

BASER The generic term encompassing any and all lasers, masers, grasers,
gravitonic-asers, &¢ that do and could exist, inasmuch as they all must
employ bosons, and al] bosons theoretically admit of such amplification.

SUPERSPACE A foundational manifold of our normal, and infinitely many other,
universes which the renowned physicist John A. Wheeler says must be taken
for granted. The concept breeds various and sundry remarkable, and indeed
bizarre, possibilities, whose nature and extent are highly imaginative
and but negligibly understood by modern physics and mathematics. For
example, there may exist some or infinitely many other universes (possessed
of arbitrarily different laws, energies, matters, dimensions, phenomena,
times, spaces, &c), these might be voyaged to (eg via black and white
holes), time itself may be travelable in either direction, and’so on
ad infinitum.

SUPERGRAVITY The hypothetical possibility that gravitation can be artificially
intensified, and thus applied.

RELATIVISTIC Pertaining to velocities near to that of light, eg 20.1c,
at which Einstenian effects become important.

SPACEPLANE An aerospace craft, or one able to both enter and leave Earth via
the atmosphere.

MASS DRIVER A linear-acceleratory or ballistic device that would shoot smal]
or microscopic objects (eg comminuted minerals), or particles, long distances
across space, and even from atmospheric or anatmospheric planetaries, thereby
achieving certain maximal economies in the cost of shipping materials, as
proposed by the physicist Gerard K. O'Neill. Massive and constant streams
of this kind might one day flow between planetaries and space.

CATOPTRICAL BALLOON Shaped balloons of titanic or astronomical size inflated
in space to create immense concave mirrors, the foci of which would be used
to propel or refine planetaries, for highly efficient power generation, or
even for weather control.

BASER RAILS Baser beams stretched between planetaries or over space to power,

directly or indirectly, commuting craft.

TERRAN Of Earth.

ACCELERATOR or LINEAR ACCELERATOR A lengthy device, whether tube or ramp, over
which a load, whether craft or material, is continuously accelerated, say in
order to attain escape velocity from a planetary, or be driven with a
land-based efficiency. Such a device can also be either vertical or aslant
with respect to the ground.

SPACIAL AUTOS Imaginary craft designed to lift mere individuals or families
into space, &r to move them about within space.

SONDED-BALLOONS Balloons dispatched atop other planetaries to monitor conditions
during continuous descent through, or other movements within, their atmosphere
or effectual ocean, the information collected by attached instruments being
transmitted out, presumably to an orbital station or relay.

DIAGALACTIC § ''Cross-galactic"', or venturing beyond the near stars, say beyond
10-100 light-years.

A.l. Artificial intelligence, the field of machines approximately as intelligent
as man, or more so; or the machines themselves.

DEMIGODS Extraterrestrial beings possessed of transhuman intelligence, character,
ability, power, or accomplishment, such as almost surely exist elsewhere in
Universe, Milky Way, or maybe nearby. Most life in Universe is apt to be
almost infinitely ahead of or behind us, and not our equal. Life hundreds
of millions of years ahead of us very likely would seem to us incomprehensible,
magical, and divine.

ARTIFICIAL SUPERMETEORS Great objects or masses dropped purposely to Earth
from space by man in the future as a transportational short-cut or a method
of engineering.

ANTIMETEORS Objects fired from Earth into space at orbital or escape velocity
without containment in needlessly expensive vessels.

INTRAJOVIAN Going within Jupiter's atmospheric envelope.

INTRASOLAR Going below Sun's surface.

FRACTIONATION Natural stratification or division into elemental, chemical,
mineralogical, &r other components, such as may distinguish Solar System
per distance from Sun, planetary size, satellitic order, atmospheric or
solid depth in a planetary, &rc. Such fractionation would be highly desirable
for, and perhaps critical to the economics of, mining in space.

TRANSNUCLEAR Involving an efficiency of mass-energy conversion in excess of
that practically or theoretically obtalnable by conventional or known fission
and fusion processes, say in excess of 4%. Some schemes have already been
suggested, and cosmology has entertained the notion that Universal oscillation
is 100% efficient, i.e. eternal.

CHEMO-SELENOGRAPHIC ATLAS An atlas giving the distribution of chemicals (minerals)
on Moon.

AGRAVITIC =Involving the nullificattonof, or shielding against, gravity, &r
suppression of inertia.

TERMITARIA Readers who are termitologists will instantly visualize those elaborate
and intricate constructions in which termites live their lives, and will
understand how future man, faced with the lethal vacua of spacial milieux, wil]
almost inevitably resort to the building of vast underground complexes, chambers,
ways, Storage places, and cities in such places as Moon, Mars, and Asteroids,
and thereby mimic the ancient termite.

GRAVITONS The gravitational quanta or particles which are supposed to exist.

LANDING ENERGY~REGENERATION SYSTEMS Systems recovering some portion of the flight
energy of a vehicle or projectile transferred, and usually wasted, in braking.
Comparable systems already operate on Earth for nonspacial purposes.

ANATMOSPHERIC Having little or no atmosphere.

MICROATMOSPHERIC Having considerably less atmosphere, and atmospheric pressure
at ground level, than Earth.

PICTOMAP A photographic montage of the surface of a planetary substituting for
a customary map and for direct exploration, given its resolution and peculiar
character. Such a pictomap may be the combined product of innumerably many
and diverse instruments, surveys, computer analyses, human designs, &c. It
may, in fact, be an atlas and comprise many alternative versions or renderings
of the landscape. It may depict both morphology and chemistry of the surface,
and either stereoscopically or holographically. Its resolution may be
absolutely incredible, the kind of thing that can be restudied under a
microscope and imaginatively walked over and reconstructed. Such pictomaps
may be creatable for all planetaries in a short time, economically, and
with almost available technology. They may use passive &r active sensors
in orbit.

PERPETUAL MOTION DEVICES or INTERPLANETARY ORBITERS Devices repeatedly circling
between planetaries, and also Sun, by relying on their gravitational fields
as their motive power and on the frictionless vacuum of space.

TRANSPLUTONIAN Of that outside, or-departing-from, Solar System.

VARIOUS REMARKS ON THE HARDSHIPS ENCOUNTERED IN READING THIS BOOK

The present order and form of the book is not at all what it will be when
the book is done. What you have instead is something escaped from a
workshop, circulated at this moment for the value its content may already
have to some, criticism, and an idea as to the nature of the work.
Complaints are frequent about the vocabulary, grammar, punctuation, and
style. For example, the coined words are viewed as unnecessary and
pretentious. The writer is conscious of the harm they do by alienating

his readership and the difficulties they present to some fixed in their
mental habits. He is particularly aware of how ugly they must cause his
beloved manuscript to appear. He nevertheless persists in his ways,
retaining the old coinages and adding new ones, for reasons which he
considers, after all, primary. He specifically feels that when a field

is first developing and someone makes an effort for the first time to
summarize and project the future of that field, an opportunity and even

an obligation exists to define the vocabulary of that field, and, in the
absence of, or case of defect in, such vocabulary this even extends to

the proposal of a new vocabulary in service to the future needs of the

field and to present discourse. Of course a certain competence and care

is presupposed in the architect of the vocabulary. The new words must

have the several virtues of being precise, accurate, formed in accordance
with the rules and traditions of etymology, mutually illuminating,
necessary, sufficient to the needs, embodying an important concept, and
relatively graceful. But it must be admitted that all words have some
defects and limitations, absolute intolerance of which would preclude the
existence of language and the ready evolution of fields of thought.
Moreover, crudities present in the new vocabulary can be removed with

time. Above all, the words | coin in this manuscript are hardly intended

to obscure matters, to impress the reader in any illusory way, or as

cheap expedients behind which there is some ignorance of science or of

the English language. They are not employed decoratively. They are not
motivated by some frivolous whimsy. | have advanced the new words for
exactly opposite reasons: as scientific instruments, as statements of

fact, as bases for better discourse, as illuminating metaphors, and as
things of beauty for their suitability. He who devises the first words

must become an object of derision by those more keen to the frail novelty of
his inventions than sensitive to the needs of the world which the brave words are
designed to answer.

An objection to the grammar is that it fs too complex and laborious.

Some readers react as if they were undergoing torture. Particularly the
endless listing of possibilities, qualifications, and aspects of things
gives umbrage to the humble reader. Readers see such listing as stuffing,
repetitious or trivial, and certainly as awkward and difficult to digest.
Yet the writer takes special pride in his listing. He sees in it an honest
coverage of the dimensions, uncertainties, and presuppositions of things,

as exemplifying unprecedented analysis and respect for the real world.

He concedes the discomfort which may be involved in accepting the complexity
of the world, but he feels the discomfort must be forgotten and the
complexity faced.

Readers are appalled at the immense paragraphs and sentences. It is doubted
that the writer has ever heard of indentations and periods, or bothers to
read what he has written. The writer replies, airily, that classical writers
achieved nobility of style with no attention to such arbitrary rules as flourish
today and pulsate in the marketing of books to increasingly undisciplined
publics. He is content to let the size and shape of his sentence and paragraph
be governed by the natural modulations of thought and the felicities of the moment.

Commentary on the preceding pair of lists.

The writer is able to suggest the distinctions between the abilities of
the human brain and current machines that he does on the basis of his
authority as a neurologist and his intense interest in computer intelligence.
The distinctions are sound. But certain ambiguities in the comparisons are
evident. These were intentional. Partly they reflect the discrepancy
between the state of the art in computer software and hardware in 1975 and
developments 1-5 decades hence, when software and hardware together will
experience immense quantitative and qualitative progress and reverse
inferior relationships to men prevailing today and in the interim. He
has scant doubt that 5 decades hence, in 2025, the computer will have
transcended human intelligence in every meaningful respect and probably to
an astronomic degree; certainly this will be the situation sometime in the
2lst century.

Partly the ambiguities just referred to reflect ambiguities inherent
in the measurements intitulated. For example, ''memory'' is a thing embodying
countless, often orthogonal, dimensions and always almost completely obscure
in its measure, or in the measures of these myriad dimensions. Therefore
it is in a way preposterous to make Pretentious comparisons between the
computer and the brain. No one knows how many "bits!! figure in human thought
or exist in human memory, ostensibly relating brain and machine--no one
has a meritorious reason for identifying a bit sum of "engrams'' exact to
a range of less than 21 orders of magnitude (or 70 octaves), and the range
could conceivably be infinite instead of finite, or permeated with far
more important considerations.

| have referred to human intuition as ''Hilbertian'’ as a stenographic
scholium for the possibility or probability that behind and basic to human
thought, memory, and insight is something like Hilbert space, or an infinite
dimensionality practically irreducible to a "bits" or information-theoretic
quantification and possibly fundamentally dissimilar to current discrete
computers. This carries with it the possibility that the memories returned
to Earth by astronauts amount to infinite gestalten, however poor their
subsequent use.

The new view of nature or world view propounded in this book, referred
to as The Efflorescent World View, complements the above and suggests that
much of nature may only at present be revealed to man, and much of Space
only to human astronauts. This of course jis an hypothesis, about which
readers will disagree. There is at least the chance that strong, subtle,
little-understood reasons exist for perpetuating men in Space or using
men and computers in sensible combinations.

A particular value of men, at least in the future, is that they can
Survey and assess large and idiosyncratic environments of data in a firsthand
and immediate way. Simultaneous speculative induction and passive and active
experimental deduction is thus possible; the compression of time for
empiriological researches is far more than linear for this quick or instantaneous
feedback, and the power with which landscape and experience are analyzed
far exceeds what would be possible in later assessing records brought back to
Earth or more or less instantaneously transmitted in awkward cybernetic ways.
This second handicap results, and has resulted, in a certain conceptual
blindness toward what obtains at the loci explored. This criticism will have
far greater force if large, permanent, professional, and theoretical teams
are eventually established at Spacial loci in place of mere machines.

Be it concluded that the debate so far over whether Programs in Space should
or could be manned or unmanned has not been very sophisticated, careful,
or decisive, and is a poor guide for policy.

PRONATALISM

Pronatalism is a favoring of human pullulation and a larger population.
It is obviously somewhat in conflict with the current antinatal philosophy.
Indeed, many people view anyone striking a pronatal stance as either
afflicted with a tragic religious bias or daffy. After all, the
assumption is that the Earth is drastically and increasingly overcrowded,
dangerous, polluted, underfed, and underresourced, and that mankind, stil}
expanding, is Proceeding toward some ghastly planetary crisis when the
limits to growth will be touched and the race decimated.

The reader of this book will be conscious that the writer is directed
by a different and far more optimistic view of things. He recognizes that
the world is Presently full of crises and undergoing a relatively
uncomfortable transition, but he sees these things as quite transitory and
the consequence of the world emerging from virtually medieval conditions
and advancing toward a higher and better civilization. He also regards
on a larger and more knowledgeable Prospect of the critical transition
being undergone by civilization. Failure to recognize this more basic
Prospect may complicate the metamorphosis and could well be disastrous.
Faith, confidence, and affirmation are necessary ingredients of a world
making the present transition. Pessimism and reaction could be deadly.

There are both trivial and profound reasons for enlarging population
now and in the future. These reasons have gane unconsidered by the current
one-sided mentality. The consequence of this may have been, and may continue
to be, untold moral harm without the slightest consciousness of the fact
on the part of ourselves. Al] the more reason, therefore, for Presenting
the pronatalist argument.

Not many years ago Europeans were gripped by a strange fear that falling
population would eradicate the race. Conditions in the world change.

Human attitudes even more so. The next age may reexperience the previous
fears of Europeans, especially since the tide of population may be ebbing

as a result of perfect, universal, and ''abused!! contraceptive technology

and as an overreaction against the present swelling of global population.

In addition, the trouble with current population size and growth may be
local, extrinsic, and fully solved in 30-50 years. tn 30-50 years the
technical and economic Progress of the world may provide the basis for

such wealth and control that the Earth may be in a position to accomodate
populations much vaster than any obtaining or foreseen now. The stupendous
human population existing in the world today would have been impossible
without the wealth created by past science and technology. There is every
reason to believe that scientific, technical, and economic progress wil]

in the future maintain Past exponential rates, and yet global population
growth is now about to decelerate of its own. As a result, relative progress
of science, technology, and the economy should assume a further, discontinuous
acceleration, and it is sensible to expect that many current problems wil]
rapidly diminish, especially since many of these problems are marginal and
temporary in nature anyway.

There are a number of positive reasons for increasing and larger populations.
Human interactions are synergistic and man's benefit to himself is a nonlinear
function of population growth. The extraordinary civilizations existing
over the world for the past 5-100 centuries, and issuing in present global
civilization, would have been impossible without the growth and magnitude
of their populations of men. Nor could such civilization arise had the

existed for 100-300 times the duration of civilization before civilization.
ing that the present population
of the world, or any lesser population, are in any way optimal for the
Flourishing of human culture and the benefit of other men. Quite the contrary,
the basis for far greater civilizations and enduring human accomp] ishment.

The prevalent if unconscious assumption is that a simple inverse relationship
exists for the quality of any populations in quantity greater than our own.

In truth, no such law, possessed of any directive value and sign, is known

to correlate population quantity and quality, except insofar as the sign is
generally positive, per supra. There are locations over the world in which
Population sizes and densities accompany seemingly inferior conditions of
life relative to some implicit scalar or vectorial optimum; there are equally
locations where such relationships exist for superior conditions. Often

the attribution of inferior conditions to dense or large populations, as

the effect of these abundant Populations, is laughable, an example being
where the standards of living in great American cities have fallen simply

as the effect of the self-governing rural or suburban migration of the higher
socioeconomic categories, so that the lower and more objectionable categories
have become concentrated in these great cities and indeed disfigured the
urban environment. Great European cities have hitherto been immune to the
tragic plight of the American cities. Even now, in the case of a great city
like New York experiencing all the problems it is, native Yorkers are devoted
to their city and spurn the countryside as dull, empty, strange, and inconvenient.
In a city like Boston, despite its average problems, a dense section like

the Italian North End has a color and safety very attractive to new residents.
In short, it as easy to defend as to criticize the life of large and dense
populations, and the critical question is the net situation and as enjoyed

by optimistic citizens, rather than those Projecting distaste and rejection
onto surprisingly neutral circumstances. To a critical degree, it can be
said that one gets out of life what he puts into it in terms of constructive,
affirmative, relaxed, and cheerful behavior: the social environment is the
projected product of the social mind. There was a day when the immensity

of Terran population was a source of delight, pride, and hope. The current
alternating weltschmerz should die with the age.

Enlargement of population has the fantastic consequence that it, in effect,
compresses time, accelerates Progress and development, and brings the future
